scoreNote: Strong (5): agrees with a clear rationale, shows why broad welfare is a more demanding and reliable indicator than elite achievement, then qualifies the claim by linking the two; well organized and persuasive.

sentences.text: When we reach for examples of national greatness, our minds turn almost reflexively to monuments and masterpieces — the cathedral, the symphony, the prize-winning scientist, the conquering general.

The statement asks us to resist that reflex, insisting that the surest indicator of a great nation lies not in the achievements of its rulers, artists, or scientists, but in the general welfare of its ordinary people.
I largely agree, because how a nation treats the mass of its citizens reveals its character far more honestly than the brilliance of a celebrated few.

sections.role: Body — Why welfare is the better indicator

sentences.text: A handful of dazzling achievements can conceal a multitude of failures.
A country may raise glittering palaces and endow magnificent galleries while the majority of its people languish in poverty, without schooling, clean water, or recourse to justice.
Such achievements measure the wealth and ambition of a narrow elite, not the health of the nation taken as a whole.
By contrast, a society in which ordinary men and women are educated, healthy, and treated with fairness has accomplished the hardest and most consequential task any nation can set itself.
Grand monuments are easy to photograph and easier still to boast about, which is exactly why they so often mislead the visitor.
Greatness shared among millions is more real, and more admirable, than greatness merely displayed by a fortunate few.

sections.role: Body — Welfare is the harder test

sentences.text: The welfare of ordinary people is, moreover, a far more demanding test than the production of celebrated individuals.

Funding a single brilliant laboratory requires only money and talent, but ensuring that tens of millions of citizens live decent lives requires fair laws, honest institutions, and effort sustained across generations.
A nation that manages the second has solved problems incomparably more complex than the raising of any monument.
It is far simpler to bankroll one celebrated laboratory than to guarantee that every child has a teacher and every patient a bed.
That is precisely why broad well-being is the surer indicator: it cannot be faked, bought cheaply, or concentrated in a single showcase for visitors to admire.
However, the statement should not be read as a wholesale dismissal of achievement.
The discoveries of scientists and the decisions of able leaders frequently improve ordinary lives, as vaccines, just laws, and new technologies raise the welfare of everyone they touch.
Achievement and welfare are not adversaries; the finest achievements are exactly those that lift the general population rather than a privileged sliver of it.
A discovery reaches its full worth only when it touches the ordinary patient, and a wise law proves itself only in the ordinary life it quietly improves.
The point is not that achievements fail to matter, but that they matter most when measured by how widely their benefits are shared.
In conclusion, the general welfare of its people is indeed the surest indicator of a nation's greatness.
Monuments and prizes can dazzle, but they can also distract us from the unglamorous question of how ordinary people actually live from one day to the next.
A truly great nation is measured less by the brilliance gathered at its summit than by the dignity it secures at its base.
